title: All 23 Indian Crew Rescued After Drone Attack Sets Tanker Ablaze Off Sochi
excerpt: The Liberian-flagged crude carrier Aframax Rio was struck by unmanned drone boats off Russia's Black Sea coast on October 6; emergency crews rescued all 23 Indian crew members with no injuries reported.
body:
• The Aframax Rio, a Liberian-flagged crude tanker sailing from the Russian port of Novorossiysk to India, was struck by unmanned drone boats off the coast of Sochi on October 6; the fire started in the cargo tanks and the ship was fully ablaze by evening.
  • Russia's transport ministry said all 23 crew members were Indian nationals and that emergency crews rescued every one of them, with preliminary information indicating no injuries.
  • Authorities closed beaches in the Sirius coastal district and urged Sochi residents to stay indoors; officials later said air and water pollutant levels remained below permissible limits.
  • No party has claimed responsibility. Russia's transport ministry attributed the strike only to an "unmanned vessel" — it is the latest in a cluster of attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea this week.

All 23 crew members of a Liberian-flagged crude oil tanker were rescued on Tuesday after unmanned drone boats struck the vessel off Russia's Black Sea coast and set it ablaze, Russian authorities said. The transport ministry said the crew was made up entirely of Indian nationals and that preliminary information indicated there were no injuries.

The vessel, identified as the Aframax Rio, was carrying crude oil from the Russian port of Novorossiysk to India — loaded nearly to capacity, according to marine tracking data — when it was hit off the coast of Sochi in the Krasnodar region. The fire broke out amidships in the cargo tanks, and burning oil spread toward the stern and spilled onto the water. By evening, the tanker was fully engulfed.

Emergency response on shore

Regional authorities in the Sirius coastal settlement, just southeast of Sochi, were the first to report the fire. Beaches in Sirius were closed to the public, and residents of Sochi were urged to keep their windows shut and stay indoors as the blaze burned offshore.

Russia's transport ministry said firefighters had sufficient equipment to tackle the fire once it became less intense, but the blaze could not be fought immediately because of its ferocity. Emergency crews brought all 23 Indian crew members ashore on Tuesday, the ministry said in a Telegram statement reported by Reuters.

Dmitry Plishkin, head of the Sirius federal territory administration, said air and water quality were being monitored continuously and that pollutant levels remained below maximum permissible concentrations, posing no threat to health.

No claim of responsibility

Russia's transport ministry attributed the strike only to an "unmanned vessel" and did not name a perpetrator. No government or armed group has publicly claimed responsibility. Unverified claims circulating in some outlets linked the attack to Ukrainian naval drones targeting sanctions-era "shadow fleet" tankers, but no official source has confirmed who carried it out.

Part of a wider pattern

The strike is the latest in a cluster of attacks on commercial shipping this week — a pattern that has put Indian seafarers repeatedly in harm's way. On the same day, Ukraine said Russian drones struck the Turkish-owned cargo ship Royad Mammadov in neutral waters of the Black Sea, killing its captain. Eleven crew members were rescued, including three Indians, one of whom was injured and treated at a hospital in Constanța, Romania. India's Ministry of External Affairs condemned that attack, saying the "targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end."

Also on October 6, drones hit two more vessels inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone: a Togolese-flagged ship that sank with crew missing, and a Palau-flagged ship left ablaze whose rescued crew included seven Indians. Separately, in the Strait of Hormuz, a projectile strike on the Panama-flagged tanker On Peace injured 12 crew members, including 11 Indians, who were evacuated to Oman.

Indian seafarers in the line of fire

India supplies one of the world's largest pools of merchant-navy crew, and this week's attacks have repeatedly put them at the center of the danger — from the Black Sea to the Gulf. Addressing the United Nations General Assembly, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar recently warned that attacks on shipping were becoming a systematic threat.

"New challenges in the maritime domain have added to longstanding ones on land. There have been attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers in the Gulf and from the Red Sea to the Black Sea. Indian seafarers have lost their lives, as have others from other nations. This is completely unacceptable."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India, at the UN General Assembly

What's next

Firefighting operations around the Aframax Rio continue, and it remains unclear when the blaze will be fully extinguished or whether the tanker can be salvaged. India's foreign ministry has not yet issued a statement specific to this incident, but given the all-Indian crew, consular coordination and repatriation arrangements will be the immediate question. Beyond that, insurers, shipowners, and the Indian importers who depend on Russian crude will be watching whether this week's attacks push more traffic — and more risk — onto the Black Sea route.
nri_angle: All 23 crew were Indian nationals — a direct safety concern for the families in India whose relatives work the Black Sea and Gulf shipping routes, and a reminder of India's outsized presence in the global merchant navy.
author: Diaspora Desk
